[h1]Overview[/h1]
This character-driven visual novel about two doctors who alter a dying man’s memories to fulfill his final wish will forever hold a special place in my heart. While the gameplay is minimal, the story more than makes up for it.

[h2]Should you buy this game?[/h2]
[b]Yes[/b] — if you enjoy narrative-focused games with emotional storytelling. However, it may not be for you if you prefer gameplay-heavy titles or a more traditional story structure.


[hr][/hr]

[h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]
[i]To the Moon[/i] is a visual novel with a few light puzzle elements. [b]There are no choices[/b], and progression is entirely story-driven as you move backward through a man’s memories to understand his life and his desire to reach the moon.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3758083484

[b]The pacing can feel slow at the beginning[/b]. I even dropped the game about an hour in during my first attempt. It takes time before the story starts to connect, but once it does, you’re left with a [b]deeply emotional, character-driven narrative[/b].

What makes the story unique is that [b]it’s told in reverse[/b], moving from later memories to earlier ones. It’s not a format you often see, and it can make the emotional context harder to grasp at times, since you’re constantly rebuilding meaning from fragments of a life you’re stepping backward through. That fragmentation is also part of what makes the ending hit as hard as it does (I cried).

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3758083636

[b]The characters and their relationships are at the center of the story[/b], with their personalities brought to life through strong dialogue. I also found the game funnier than expected in places, which helps balance out the heavier themes.

The pixel art and music are another highlight. Both are beautiful and…
Not much gameplay but yes ... I do recommend this. It is slow at times. But idk. It is worthy of your 4 hours.
bit slow at times but the ending was worth it

This game tells a story at a pace that seems too slow at first, but hits you perfectly when it hits. At the start, I was annoyed with the "game" parts of the game - the puzzles are fine but thoroughly unconnected to what the game is actually doing. While the other main game mechanic - searching around the room for items that can be used to connect memories - was a slog to start out with, I do think it helped you take more notice of details and slowly coming to appreciate why those things mattered worked well for the the game. The story is simple in some ways but still beautiful. Characters mostly all have more depth than they initially appear to. Stick with this one.
A beautiful game with a wonderful art style and music. Just buy it, play it and don't be discouraged by the slowly building story. You won't regret it!

The game is a little boring to start, but the story surrounding it is fantastic. I think they did a wonderful job of portraying a story and making you feel all the emotions within the story. The controls are a little irritating with having to constantly click and reset the click over and over but overall I really enjoyed the game and highly recommend it to anyone that likes story games with a well driven story.

claims.claim: Reviewers report that the gameplay is minimal, consisting mostly of walking, interacting with objects, and solving simple puzzles.

citations.review_text:
To the Moon was, honestly, a very beautiful experience for me. I happily recommend this one, especially if you need a solid cry.

The gameplay is at times janky, but certainly still playable, and I mean it when I say the rough edges didn't matter to me at all by the end. The story is so genuine and heartfelt that I find it somewhat hard to explain how hard it hit - I'll admit that I ugly cried through basically the entire ending and yaknow what?? It wasn't even embarrassing. The game earned every one of those tears if you ask me. This game is imo an absolute MUST play if you like story-heavy games. It's only about 4 hours long and I highly recommend finishing it in one sitting if you can =))

The game itself has you playing as two scientists who essentially dig through memories to craft a dream for dying patients, helping them "live out" an event they wish they had experienced in life. In this case, you're helping an elderly man named Johnny fulfill his last wish of going to the moon. You explore through various memories of his, slowly uncovering his whole life story to understand why he wishes to visit the moon, and learning how you can make that happen for him on his deathbed. Gameplay is essentially an interactive visual novel with a few simple puzzles, so don't expect anything crazy here, but I think the simplicity and fantastic soundtrack do exactly what they need to to help bolster this very poignant story about love, family, and loss.

Let me start by stating that I love pixel art, rich soundtracks, and narrative-driven titles. To the Moon checks all three boxes.

I first played this game in 2018. While its beautiful soundtrack stayed with me over the years, most of the plot had faded from memory. During a recent multi-hour train ride, I was scrolling through my Steam Deck library and rediscovered this gem. I decided to give it another shot, playing through both the main game and the two free "Sigmund Minisodes" DLCs.

There is so much to love here. It’s a deeply emotional story about life, love, family, and loss, following a dying man and his late wife, alongside two doctors who rarely agree on anything but always have each other's backs when it counts. The soundtrack, in particular, is stunning and carries the weight of the narrative effortlessly.

Just don't expect traditional gameplay. The experience consists almost entirely of searching for objects, clicking through environments, and solving the occasional light puzzle. It leans far closer to an interactive visual novel or walking simulator than a standard video game.

Because it's relatively short, it never overstays its welcome. For me, replaying it was an absolute pleasure. The optional minisodes also add a fantastic touch, fleshing out Sigmund Corp., exploring its employees, and leaving you with a few intriguing mysteries to chew on.

If you enjoy story-driven experiences with great art and music, and don't mind minimal gameplay, you owe it to yourself to give To the Moon a try.

This is a short and fun game. Although I went in expecting a very good story, I found exactly that… but it was even better constructed than I had expected.

“To The Moon” is very light and easy to play. It is fun and relaxing. The fact that it is a short game also keeps it from feeling repetitive. The game just feels right.

The gameplay is very simple. You only have to walk, listen to dialogues, and find memories throughout the scenes… and that is basically it. Yes, you have to solve a puzzle every time you change memories, but they are so easy that I would not categorize the game as a puzzle game. There is no combat, except for one brief section, the exploration is good (even though the game is linear), and, for me, the only two bugs I encountered were related to the game's only achievement and with a word writing puzzle. The solution for this last one was to launch the game in the classic version. 

The only achievement is awarded for beating the game, but after I finished it, I did not unlock it. The solution was to follow a guide on how to get it, and in less than 10 minutes everything was working properly.

If you like short, relaxing games with a great soundtrack and a good story, you should definitely give it a try.

[h1] To The Moon [/h1] (no spoilers)
[i] A story about two doctors traversing backwards through a dying man's memories to artificially fulfil his last wish. [/i]

This was a short game, about 4h, the game is highly praised and with reason! The premise is simple, fulfil the wish of a dying man, to do that we have to go through his memories to find the reason he wants that specific wish, and while we do that, we learn about his entire life. Its something that I wasn't expecting to get that invested into, but oh how wrong I was... from the very start- the characters we play as were very lively, every line, every joke, every cheeky comment, they all felt super organic, the writing is something I am not able to praise enough! Not only the character writing but the way the story is laid out in front of us, and the way both the doctors as well as us the player, each slowly learn and connect the dots to our own conclusions, its simply something that captures you in the moment, and reflecting about it afterwards makes me appreciate it even more. On top of that, as mentioned, the characters are incredibly well written, and the jokes, even though some are very silly- they feel organic, like I believe this character would say this at this time!  For a game to make me care so much about the life and wishes of an old man at the brink of death, literally no words to describe it.

The gameplay is very simple, mostly walking and interacting with stuff, but we get a puzzle in between memories- and the puzzles were good, they weren't hard, but also not free, they just felt nice as little breaks in between segments.

The music was simple, yet always hit when it needed to, just how much can you convey with only 2 notes?

claims.claim: Reviewers report finding navigation and knowing where to go confusing at times.

citations.review_text:
The title sounds like it’s shilling crypto lmao.

It was a bittersweet story, though a bit convoluted and it had way too much comedic relief that sometimes undercut the drama. As a game it was poor, buggy, often confusing about where to go or what to do, with aimless wandering possible and a pace that felt way too slow. Walking, talking and transitions all dragged, and the only real minigame was that really lame tile flip puzzle. Great music though.

Overall it was still a positive experience despite the issues.

At first glance, the game has a strange simplicity. Two doctors use a memory altering machine to enter a dying man's mind to fulfill his request of visiting the moon. A request whose reason remains unknown to him. From the millions of possible requests he could have asked for, this is the one he chose. As you visit memories from different points in time, being lost, not understanding them and the only option you have is to keep going until you begin connecting the dots. Leaving you with an unexpected emotional realization once the bigger picture finally comes together.

With little to no actual gameplay, this game is still one of my favorites. Perhaps it should be my favorite. There are some things in life we take for granted without knowing. Things that need to be appreciated. No matter how bad things get, there are always people worse off.

At the time of writing this it's been about 7 months since I finished the game yet I felt like writing a review is needed as time passed. If this lands on anybody's screen, the game is worth it and a start to an amazing series.

Confusing, empathy and happiness is the only way of describing this game.
The story was amazingly well written and combined with the soundtrack made everything so much better.

My only downside (which is probably due to my peanut brain) is that it wasn't always clear to know where to go.
Despite that I still enjoyed it and I cherished every moment of it.

A tortuously bad premise: a pair of doctors work for a company that rewires dying people's memories to make them believe things that never happened so that they can... die happy? Hopefully these patients don't recover and have a head full of lies that have to be undone ("No I did go to the moon!"). And the story really just gets worse from there. The two main doctor characters are nearly the most unlikable and unnecessary characters in the lot. The caretaker and her children serve no point. A lot of the dialogue is bickering and bantering. I think there were many lines by characters that were intended to be funny, but they are of a caliber that don't even warrant an eye-roll. The whole narrative and exposition plod along at a pace that could only be deemed comfortable by people who don't value their time.

The execution of the game as a point-and-click walking simulator is below average. The graphics are fine if you're looking for a 16-bit retro experience, but they contribute to the mess of knowing where to click which seems to be the game's only consistent challenge. Although I'm not convinced this was ever really meant to present any challenge to the player. You'll get to the end with enough clicks; there is no failing.

There are a few nice, if not repetitive, musical pieces (the game gets meta and points this out). Anything outside of the tender emotional pieces fall flat. The tense music often feels out of place.

Don't fall for the hype. Do yourself a favor and avoid. There are more genuinely emotionally touching games than this. Check out a youtube video if you're curious about the music, but you'll hear most of what the game has to offer in the trailer video.

claims.claim: Reviewers highlight the soundtrack as a standout, beautiful element of the experience.

citations.review_text:
To the Moon was, honestly, a very beautiful experience for me. I happily recommend this one, especially if you need a solid cry.

The gameplay is at times janky, but certainly still playable, and I mean it when I say the rough edges didn't matter to me at all by the end. The story is so genuine and heartfelt that I find it somewhat hard to explain how hard it hit - I'll admit that I ugly cried through basically the entire ending and yaknow what?? It wasn't even embarrassing. The game earned every one of those tears if you ask me. This game is imo an absolute MUST play if you like story-heavy games. It's only about 4 hours long and I highly recommend finishing it in one sitting if you can =))

The game itself has you playing as two scientists who essentially dig through memories to craft a dream for dying patients, helping them "live out" an event they wish they had experienced in life. In this case, you're helping an elderly man named Johnny fulfill his last wish of going to the moon. You explore through various memories of his, slowly uncovering his whole life story to understand why he wishes to visit the moon, and learning how you can make that happen for him on his deathbed. Gameplay is essentially an interactive visual novel with a few simple puzzles, so don't expect anything crazy here, but I think the simplicity and fantastic soundtrack do exactly what they need to to help bolster this very poignant story about love, family, and loss.

I played this game for 4 hours, which is the total time it takes to complete the entire campaign. I unlocked 1 out of the 1 achievement (which unlocks automatically right after you finish the story). I picked it up on sale for just $1.

Story
The story, concept, and overall narrative execution are an absolute 10 out of 10. I genuinely loved this story from start to finish. It hits exceptionally hard on an emotional level—I may or may not have cried during it, but it is an unforgettable narrative.

Gameplay & Mechanics
The gameplay is nothing too special, but it doesn't need to be. It does just enough to keep you engaged and make you feel like you are directly part of the world, without overcomplicating things or doing more than it should.

Music & Soundtrack
The soundtrack is phenomenal. The music is perfect from top to bottom and got me really emotional at one point. It does a huge amount of heavy lifting to elevate the mood and impact of the story.

Characters
Both of the main leads—Dr. Neil Watts and Dr. Eva Rosalene—are written so well. Their dynamic and dialogue keep you invested in their mission throughout the entire game.

Visuals & Art Direction
I love pixel art, and the visual style here is fantastic. It gave off great vibes and complemented the story's atmosphere perfectly.

Technical Aspects
The game is extremely lightweight on hardware. You can play this on an old laptop and still get the best possible experience. A great bonus is that it is natively available on Mac, so MacBook users can run it seamlessly.

Final Thoughts
This game is an absolute masterpiece in narrative design. Getting a story and soundtrack of this caliber for a dollar felt like a total steal, and I would do it all over again in a heartbeat.

Watched PewDiePie play this over a decade ago, sooooo glad I finally experienced it myself.

Heartfelt story, absolutely fell in love with its visuals as a pixel art fan, and the soundtrack is simply beautiful. One of those games that quietly stays with you long after.

This game proved to me that you don't need breathtaking graphics to build a masterpiece, a powerful story and a moving soundtrack are more than enough to create an unforgettable experience
The piano melodies in this game weren't just background music, they played directly on our heartstrings, driving our emotions and tears with every single scene.
The ending left a profound impact on me taking me through a warm emotional journey that completely changed how I look at memories.

I highly recommend it to anyone who truly appreciates warm, story driven and emotionally moving games.

Kaka.

I had the privilege of spending more than a year in a hospital as part of my studies. Observing people whose burdensome sicknesses threaten the very bane of their existence; witnessing numerous end-of-life cases where family members are torn between extending their loved one’s life through painfully aggressive treatments or sedating them slowly to death in an effort to alleviate their pain; listening to countless life stories of patients that are filled with grief, melancholy, and regret... One thing that was common in all those cases and moments of vulnerability was how people tried to piece together events or snapshots of their lives and try to weave them into a meaningful story... of their lives. To The Moon is a very creative and touching interpretation of this aspect of the human condition, which is why I cannot recommend the game enough.

Since there is not much of a 'gameplay' involved, the one and strongest punch of the game is its story that is aided so well with the amazing soundtrack and occasionally striking art. The game creates a world in which Sigmund Corp. is heavily involved in advanced care planning through its technology that can create artificial memories and fulfil wishes of clients who are breathing the last days of their life; a very individualized form of a 'noble lie'. The story centers on two of its employees trying to traverse and make sense of the memories of a client in order to fulfill his rather vague wish of going to the moon. Although the game is rather short, the story takes its time to unfold while not having much of a downfall in its build-up. The non-linear aspect of storytelling constantly kept me hooked and curious while the twists and turns in the plot made it a rather emotional roller coaster which ended with me having teary eyes. 

One thing that I felt quite uneasy and at times bothered by was the conversations and interactions between the two Sigmund Corp. employees, Dr. Eva Rosalene and Dr. Neil Watts, as they felt very l…
The only game to ever make me cry, and I'll recommend it to everyone forever and ever.

To the Moon sits in a very distinct category as far as games go. It is focused on story and emotion. The game mechanics are not important; you are not being punished for doing anything wrong during a puzzle, so leave your competitive side at the door when you press play.

The game takes some ideas from Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, but it still feels original. This comparison should give away the main concept of the game. If you loved the movie, I am sure you will also love this game.

The music, composed by Kan Gao, also the creator of the game, is amazing. It fits the game perfectly; it never feels boring, even if you stay in the same scene for minutes. The songs have a calming, homey feel that never becomes annoying despite their repetition.

The art matches the story; it always surprises me how pixel art can show a character's emotions so well. The colours remind me of autumn, and everything feels very atmospheric. It's a beautiful game to look at.

I want to underline that, as with all different mediums of art, games can also have an emotional impact, and To the Moon will work your tear ducts to the maximum. Have some tissues ready, just in case.
A beautiful game with a wonderful art style and music. Just buy it, play it and don't be discouraged by the slowly building story. You won't regret it!

The art style is fitting for the atmosphere, and the premise is believable enough that you feel this could happen in our lifetimes. 

It’s not often I sit at the end of a game and say “wow”. This game did it for me. 

Give this game a try. It takes 3.5-5 hours to complete and you will unlock the single achievement once you complete the game. 

Go in blind, and enjoy the experience.
This is one of the best indie games ever. The story, music and conclusion are near perfection. All that managed in just roughly 4 hours.

Heartfelt story, absolutely fell in love with its visuals as a pixel art fan, and the soundtrack is simply beautiful. One of those games that quietly stays with you long after.

I'm obsessed with the storyline and how relatable and not relatable each character is. Eva, Neil, River, John, Nick. Izzy, all of them are their own and have such personal touches. I cried a few times during the playthrough and I think that makes it so much better. I can feel the love and creativity put into the game and the thought put into it. The art style reminds me a lot of sea of stars and its one of my favorite ways games add creativity. I 100% recommend this game to anyone and everyone. If you really like story based indie sort of games I think this is an amazing one.
If you have a few hours spare one evening and want a great emotional story with a charming retro pixel art style. This is your game. 10/10.

I can't find the right words to describe the emotional experience this game gave me. Touching, bittersweet and deeply nostalgic without even relating to it. Was hooked on the storyline and was always anticipating the next scene, while also savouring the present ones. LOVED the way the 2 doctors interacted with each other, made the journey nicer and got some laughs out of it. Anyway, this game will leave some type of emotional memento on you. I highly recommend it.
ALSO lovely soundtrack and art style.

This game is a masterpiece! A beautiful work of art, with an incredibly well-written narrative and a pretty pixel art style! As an aspiring writer, I feel like a learned a lot from it and just really appreciated how well-told it was! I'm also aware how incredibly difficult it is to write a narrative in non-chrological order, so the fact that this one is told BACKWARDS is a testament to its writing! It's so easy to get lost in this story and to feel connected to the characters and their struggle. So many parts feel so real and tragic and beautiful. And other times it breaks up that sadness with some really funny moments, and it balances both the humor and drama perfectly. 

I 100% bawled at the end and if you enjoy well-written narratives I suggest you play it and bawl with me!!

A beautiful and intimate story. With humor and wit, we learn about the life of a man who dreams of traveling to the Moon. The character dynamics and the lovingly crafted pixel art accompany us on this journey. While I personally felt the puzzle segments weren't really necessary, they never got in the way either. Those who pay attention between the lines will be rewarded.

A tortuously bad premise: a pair of doctors work for a company that rewires dying people's memories to make them believe things that never happened so that they can... die happy? Hopefully these patients don't recover and have a head full of lies that have to be undone ("No I did go to the moon!"). And the story really just gets worse from there. The two main doctor characters are nearly the most unlikable and unnecessary characters in the lot. The caretaker and her children serve no point. A lot of the dialogue is bickering and bantering. I think there were many lines by characters that were intended to be funny, but they are of a caliber that don't even warrant an eye-roll. The whole narrative and exposition plod along at a pace that could only be deemed comfortable by people who don't value their time.

The execution of the game as a point-and-click walking simulator is below average. The graphics are fine if you're looking for a 16-bit retro experience, but they contribute to the mess of knowing where to click which seems to be the game's only consistent challenge. Although I'm not convinced this was ever really meant to present any challenge to the player. You'll get to the end with enough clicks; there is no failing.

There are a few nice, if not repetitive, musical pieces (the game gets meta and points this out). Anything outside of the tender emotional pieces fall flat. The tense music often feels out of place.

Don't fall for the hype. Do yourself a favor and avoid. There are more genuinely emotionally touching games than this. Check out a youtube video if you're curious about the music, but you'll hear most of what the game has to offer in the trailer video.

citations.review_text:
I was not expecting to completely fall in love with this game. I booted it up planning to play for one hour, but ended up completing it in about 3 and a half hours.

To The Moon is a story-driven adventure like no other, at least not that I've seen. You play as 2 doctors, which you switch between, but in the beginning you kind of get a choice of who you'll be playing most as. I chose Rosalene.

Your goal is to grant your client's last wish, no matter what it is. You can probably guess from the game's title what our dying man desires. To do that, you need to find out why exactly he wished for that, and thus you travel through his memories until you put it together.

The graphics are very old-school RPG-like, which I wasn't too keen on at first, but they quickly grew on me. I attribute that to how good the storytelling is. There is also a puzzle element to it, but I won't go into detail. They were quite simple, but I looked forward to each one.

By the end of it I was crying like a baby. It's such a sappy but beautiful story.

Something that intrigued me was the neurodiversity mentions. However, I didn't quite like how they framed it. All I will say is that they tapped into the struggles that come with being neurodivergent, which is great, but at times it felt like they were reducing the characters to just that.

PROS:
- incredible storytelling
- provides lots of laughs
- plenty of tears
CONS:
- outdated graphics
- the controls
- the portrayal of neurodiversity

This game has been sitting in my Steam library since it first released, and I finally decided to give it a go in an effort to clear out some shorter titles during my limited free time. I am incredibly glad I did.
Gameplay-wise, To the Moon is very basic. There are only a few simple puzzles and light mechanics to worry about from time to time, but the gameplay isn't the point here. The true draw is the touching, often tragic story of Johnny. I was completely caught off guard by how deeply it affected me, and I was moved to tears at multiple points during my playthrough. Supporting the narrative are the two main scientists, who share a great banter—even if some of their quips can feel a bit juvenile or slightly lost in translation at times.
Ultimately, To the Moon feels less like a traditional video game and more like a interactive piece of fiction. It is a rare feat; very few books or even movies—which have the luxury of cinematic tricks to pull at your heartstrings—have ever managed to deliver an emotional gut-punch this powerful.
It was worth every single minute. Now that the credits have rolled, I'll definitely be setting aside some time to dive into the additional content and the sequels.

## Why

- The memento puzzles are kinda neat brain teasers
- The premise of the game is an interesting concept

## Why Not

- Somewhat incoherent story in a story-driven game
- They don't do as much as they could with the premise
- Nice pixel art ruined by constant filters
- Dialogue can be forced at times

## Impressions

I've heard a lot of good things about this one but just don't get it. The premise is cool but underutilized in favour of a focus on characters who just aren't that interesting and their mountains of sad experiences. There's a twist(?) near the end which was somewhat surprising, but when I stepped back to think about it I couldn't think of a reason it needed to be in the story. It didn't affect the main plot in any way; just another bad time on the bad time pile.

It definitely has some positives, I did finish it after all, but I just don't see what makes it special. Without the expectations I had going in I would've just walked away from this thinking 'huh, that was ok I guess' but IMO there are much better narrative experiences in games these days, especially games which're exclusively story-focused like this.
